This chart is about population survival ages, meaning the age that different shares of a birth cohort would reach if they experienced the death rates observed in a given year.
The chart image specifically shows France from 1816 to 2023, while the data table also provides recent cross-country values for 2022 to 2024.
It belongs to the demography and population health domain.
The source is Our World in Data, drawing on Alvarez & Vaupel (2023) and the Human Mortality Database (2025).
In France in 2023, the top 1% survival age is 102.67 years, the median 50% survival age is 86.13 years, and the 99% survival age is 32.79 years.

The percentile labels work in an inverted way relative to rank: the 99% line corresponds to the age by which 99% of people would have died and only 1% would still be alive, while the top 1% line corresponds to the age reached by the longest-surviving 1%.
These are period survival ages, not predictions for an actual birth cohort’s future lifetime under changing mortality conditions.
They answer a counterfactual question: if a person were born in that year and faced that year’s age-specific death rates throughout life, how long would different parts of the population survive?

The chart image title names France, 1816 to 2023, but the metadata table is broader and includes multiple countries with mostly recent years; this means the image and table serve different purposes: historical trend for one country and recent benchmark comparison across countries.
The chart does not provide sex-specific, socioeconomic, or cause-of-death breakdowns, so it cannot by itself explain why one country or period performs better than another.
